extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy, colonial administration, and trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging the effects of colonial union, mercantile regulation, and monopolies on national wealth and colonial welfare. Focuses on representation, distribution of capital (stock), monopoly effects, and proper public policy toward trade and colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation from every part of the empire
rubrics_metrics.description: The assembly which deliberates and decides concerning the affairs of every part of the empire, in order to be properly informed, ought certainly to have representatives from every part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union of colonies with the mother country would complete the constitution by providing representation; practical difficulties in execution may exist but are not insurmountable. Representative presence ensures the assembly is properly informed about all parts of the empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional representation by taxation/produce
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of American representatives were to be in proportion to the produce of American taxation, the number of people to be managed would increase exactly in proportion to the means of managing them, and the means of managing to the number of people to be managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportional representation tied to fiscal contribution preserves constitutional balance between monarchical and democratical parts and prevents overturning of the balance by a sudden influx of representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation protects distant constituents despite distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Their representatives in parliament ... would easily be able to protect them from all oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance does not much weaken dependency of representative on constituents; representatives have incentive to complain of abuses and protect remote parts, so geographic distance is not itself sufficient reason to fear oppression if representation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seat of empire follows economic contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The seat of the empire would then naturally remove itself to that part of the empire which contributed most to the general defence and support of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As colonies grow in wealth, population, and improvement, political centrality may shift toward the most contributory region; policy should account for changing economic weight within an empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual commerce tends to be beneficial overall
rubrics_metrics.description: By uniting in some measure the most distant parts of the world, by enabling them to relieve one another’s wants, to increase one another’s enjoyments, and to encourage one another’s industry, their general tendency would seem to be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While commercial contact spreads benefits (knowledge, improvements) and fosters equality of force that overawes injustice, the immediate consequences for native populations have often been disastrous because of European superiority; long-term benefits depend on balance of power and mutual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile system's objective and its expansion by discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the object of that system to enrich a great nation, rather by trade and manufactures than by the improvement and cultivation of land ... Two new worlds have been opened to their industry ... the market of one of them growing still greater and greater every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery expanded markets and magnified the mercantile system’s influence by turning commercial towns into manufacturers and carriers for much larger markets; this scale change affects national economic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial consumption often benefits third countries
rubrics_metrics.description: The colonies of Spain and Portugal ... give more real encouragement to the industry of other countries than to that of Spain and Portugal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: colonial consumption of linen is mainly supplied by France, Flanders, Holland, and Germany, transferring capital and revenue abroad; home country may only enjoy the spending of profits, not the productive re-distribution of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive-trade regulations often hurt the enforcing country
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the regulations by which each nation endeavours to secure to itself the exclusive trade of its own colonies, are frequently more hurtful to the countries in favour of which they are established, than to those against which they are established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: merchants forced to route trade through a metropolis (Hamburg → London → America) suffer slower returns and lower profits; home merchants whose stock is drawn into monopolistic employments may harm national advantage by tying up capital in slow-return enterprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly is the central engine of the mercantile system
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopoly of one kind or another, indeed, seems to be the sole engine of the mercantile system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopolies establish exclusive rights (either excluding other nations or confining trade to an exclusive company), which distort capital allocation and create incentives contrary to the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of monopoly and their distinct effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In the trade to America ... a different sort of monopoly. ... in the East Indies ... subjected to an exclusive company. Monopolies of this kind are properly established against the very nation which erects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First kind: exclusion of other nations from colonial trade — hurts excluded nations and attracts stock to the monopolized trade. Second kind: domestic exclusive companies — may harm the home country by restricting participation and encouraging waste/fraud in management; effects differ by national wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies of the first kind attract excess stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolies of the first kind always attract to the particular trade in which they are established a greater proportion of the stock of the society than what would go to that trade of its own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By denying competition, such monopolies draw capital into a specific trade beyond its natural level, causing misallocation and social harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies of the second kind have wealth-dependent effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolies of the second kind may sometimes attract stock ... and sometimes repel it ... In poor countries, they naturally attract towards that trade more stock than would otherwise go to it. In rich countries, they naturally repel from it a good deal of stock which would otherwise go to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sweden and Denmark only sent ships due to monopoly incentives; Holland's limited company stock repelled the abundant Dutch capital which would otherwise flow into East Indies trade under free conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private mercantile stock naturally prefers near, frequent-return employments
rubrics_metrics.description: The mercantile stock of every country naturally courts in this manner the near, and shuns the distant employment: naturally courts the employment in which the returns are frequent, and shuns that in which they are distant and slow; naturally courts the employment which ... can maintain the greatest quantity of productive labour in the country ... and shuns that in which it can maintain there the smallest quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners favor employments that provide quicker returns and sustain domestic productive labor; this private inclination typically aligns with public interest absent distortions, producing an approximately optimal distribution of capital among employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: High profits signal underinvestment and public interest to redirect stock
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in any one of those distant employments, ... the profit should happen to rise somewhat higher than what is sufficient to balance the natural preference ... this superiority of profit will draw stock from those nearer employments, till the profits of all return to their proper level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevated profits indicate that a distant employment is understocked; public interest requires some capital withdrawal from nearer employments to correct prices and relieve oppression caused by artificially high prices of necessary goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derangement of natural stock distribution is socially hurtful
rubrics_metrics.description: Every derangement of the natural distribution of stock is necessarily hurtful to the society in which it takes place; whether it be by repelling from a particular trade the stock which would otherwise go to it, or by attracting towards a particular trade that which would not otherwise come to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both attractions and repulsions of capital caused by regulations or monopolies produce losses: either insufficient development of some trades or inappropriate diversion of scarce capital from more necessary domestic uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive companies are not necessary for establishing East India trade
rubrics_metrics.description: That such companies are not in general necessary for carrying on the East India trade, is sufficiently demonstrated by the experience of the Portuguese, who enjoyed almost the whole of it for more than a century together, without any exclusive company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a nation is 'ripe' for the trade, private merchants naturally divide capital among principal and subordinate branches; colonies and settlements can be safe under sovereign protection rather than company monopolies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid diverting capital into distant trades if nation is not ripe
rubrics_metrics.description: If ... that country was not ripe for that trade, and that it would do better to buy for some time, even at a higher price, from other European nations, the East India goods it had occasion for, than to import them itself directly from the East Indies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When domestic capital is scarce, forcing it into slow-return distant trade can be worse than paying higher prices for imports; the opportunity cost in lost domestic productive labor can exceed the price premium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial administration should increase annual produce and open markets
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the revenue of the people, therefore, the greater the annual produce of their land and labour, the more they can afford to the sovereign. It is his interest, therefore, to increase as much as possible that annual produce. ... It is the interest of such a sovereign, therefore, to open the most extensive market for the produce of his country, to allow the most perfect freedom of commerce ... and upon this account to abolish, not only all monopolies, but all restraints upon the transportation of the home produce ... upon its exportation to foreign countries, or upon the importation of goods of any kind for which it can be exchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign policy should favor free commerce and open markets to enlarge the market for domestic produce, thereby increasing both quantity and value of output and the sovereign's revenue (especially where revenue depends on land-rent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Companies acting as sovereigns will favor merchant profits over sovereign revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: A company of merchants, are, it seems, incapable of considering themselves as sovereigns, even after they have become such. Trade, or buying in order to sell again, they still consider as their principal business ... They endeavour ... to reduce ... the surplus produce of those countries to what is barely sufficient for supplying their own demand, or to what they can expect to sell in Europe, with such a profit as they may think reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchant-governors often treat sovereign authority as an appendix to commerce, restricting markets and production to raise short-term profit at the expense of long-term revenue and the welfare of the subject country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolistic governance produces destructive local policies
rubrics_metrics.description: In the spice islands, the Dutch are said to burn all the spiceries which a fertile season produces, beyond what they expect to dispose of in Europe ... they give a premium to those who collect the young blossoms ... which this savage policy has now, it is said, almost completely extirpated. ... The servants of the company have ... order[ed] a peasant to plough up a rich field of poppies, and sow it with rice, or some other grain. The pretence was, to prevent a scarcity of provisions; but the real reason, to give the chief an opportunity of selling at a better price a large quantity of opium which he happened then to have upon hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show company agents manipulating production (burning, extirpation, forced crop-switching) to protect monopoly profits, with long-term destructive effects on population, agriculture, and colony welfare; such practices are directly contrary to sovereign/public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive companies stunt colony growth and settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The genius of exclusive companies, besides, is unfavourable, it has already been observed, to the growth of new colonies, and has probably been the principal cause of the little progress which they have made in the East Indies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By concentrating trade privileges and discouraging private settlement and open commerce, companies impede the establishment of thriving, self-sustaining colonies comparable to those in America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies create illusion of valuable prize but harm national capital allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: At first sight, no doubt, the monopoly of the great commerce of America naturally seems to be an acquisition of the highest value ... The dazzling splendour of the object, however, the immense greatness of the commerce, is the very quality which renders the monopoly of it hurtful ... makes one employment ... absorb a much greater proportion of the capital of the country than what would otherwise have gone to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, tempting monopolies concentrate capital into single employments, crowding out more appropriate domestic investments and producing overall loss despite apparent gains.
